title: Normal is home
concept: Vim starts in Normal mode, where the letters on your keyboard are commands, not text. `i` opens Insert mode so you can actually type. `Esc` always brings you home to Normal. Two doors, one room — that is the whole idea.
document:
# Trip notes

Reykjavik in March. Bring layers.

steps.instruction: Press `i` to open Insert mode.
steps.hint: Just the letter `i` — it means "insert here".

steps.instruction: You are in Insert mode. Press `Esc` to come home to Normal.
steps.hint: `Esc` sits top-left. When you are not sure where you are, press it.

title: Move without leaving home row
concept: `h` `j` `k` `l` are your arrow keys, sitting under your right hand: `h` left, `j` down, `k` up, `l` right. Same four directions, no reach across the keyboard.

outcomePreview.caption: four directions under your right hand — the ghosts show where each lands

steps.instruction: Move down one line with `j`.
steps.hint: `j` points down — the letter even hangs below the line.

steps.instruction: Step one character to the right with `l`.
steps.hint: `l` is the rightmost of the four — so it moves right.

steps.instruction: Step back up a line with `k`.
steps.hint: `k` kicks up. It is the neighbour just above `j`'s direction.

steps.instruction: Step one character to the left with `h`.
steps.hint: `h` is the leftmost of the four — so it moves left.

title: Five doors into Insert
concept: One idea, five doors. `a` appends after the cursor, `I` jumps to the first real character of the line, `A` to the end of it, `o` opens a fresh line below and `O` one above. Where you want to type decides which door you use.

outcomePreview.caption: five new doors, plus the i you already know — the ghosts show where each one lands

doors.note: jumps to the first real character of the line
jumps to the end of the line

steps.instruction: Press `a` to start typing just AFTER the cursor.
steps.hint: `a` is for append. `i` would put you before the cursor instead.

steps.instruction: Press `I` to jump to the first real character of this indented line and type there.
steps.hint: Capital `I` — hold Shift. It skips the indent and lands on the `s`.

steps.instruction: Press `A` to jump to the end of this line and type there.
steps.hint: Capital `A` — hold Shift. It is append, but all the way to the end.

steps.instruction: Press `o` to open a brand new line below this one.
steps.hint: Lowercase `o` opens the new line underneath and drops you on it.

steps.instruction: Press `O` to open a new line ABOVE this one.
steps.hint: Capital `O` — hold Shift. Same door as `o`, opening upward.

title: How to leave
concept: `:` opens a command line at the bottom of the screen. `:w` writes the file, `:q` quits, and `:wq` does both. Press Return to run it. Nobody is ever trapped in Vim again.

# Draft post

steps.instruction: Save the file: type `:w` and press Return.
steps.hint: Colon first, then `w` for write, then Return to run it.

steps.instruction: Quit: type `:q` and press Return.
steps.hint: `q` is quit. `Esc` backs out of the `:` prompt if you change your mind.

steps.instruction: Do both at once: type `:wq` and press Return.
steps.hint: `:wq` is just `w` and `q` said together — write, then quit.

title: Move by words, not letters
concept: A word is a noun Vim understands. `w` jumps to the start of the next word, `b` back to the start of the previous one, `e` to the end of the one you are on. This is the first real speed-up: stop pressing `l` forty times.

# Meeting notes

Ship the beta before Friday.

steps.instruction: Jump forward one word with `w`.
steps.hint: `w` is for word. It lands on the FIRST letter of the next one.

steps.instruction: Jump back one word with `b`.
steps.hint: `b` is for back — the mirror image of `w`.

steps.instruction: Jump to the END of this word with `e`.
steps.hint: `e` is for end. `w` goes to the next word's start; `e` stops on this word's last letter.

title: Anchors: line ends and file ends
concept: Five anchors you will use forever: `0` the very start of a line, `^` its first real character, `$` its end, `gg` the top of the file and `G` the bottom. Big jumps, one keystroke.

steps.instruction: Jump to the end of this line with `$`.
steps.hint: `$` means "end of line" — the same `$` you may know from search boxes.

steps.instruction: Jump back to column zero with `0`.
steps.hint: `0` is the number zero — the zeroth column, indentation included.

steps.instruction: Now use `^` to land on the first real character instead, skipping the indent.
steps.hint: `^` (Shift-6) skips leading spaces; `0` does not.

steps.instruction: Jump to the top of the file with `gg`.
steps.hint: Two `g`s in a row. Press them one after the other, not together.

steps.instruction: Jump to the bottom of the file with `G`.
steps.hint: Capital `G` — hold Shift. It is `gg`'s opposite end.

title: Fly to a character
concept: `f` flies along this line to a character you name: `fk` lands ON the next `k`. `t` stops just before it, and capital `F` searches backwards. Aim at a letter and you are there.
document:
# Errands

pick up the keys at 4pm

steps.instruction: Fly to the first `k` on this line: press `f` then `k`.
steps.hint: `f` waits for one more key — the character to fly to.

steps.instruction: Stop just BEFORE the `4`: press `t` then `4`.
steps.hint: `t` is "till" — it stops one character short of the target.

steps.instruction: Search backwards to the previous `k`: press `F` then `k`.
steps.hint: Capital `F` — hold Shift. Same idea as `f`, aimed the other way.

title: Delete one, undo one
concept: `x` deletes the single character under the cursor — think of it as crossing something out. `u` undoes your last change. Nothing you do here is permanent, which is exactly why you can experiment.

steps.instruction: The cursor sits on the doubled `k`. Press `x` to cross it out.
steps.hint: `x` deletes exactly the character under the block cursor.

steps.instruction: The `k` is gone. Press `u` to undo and bring it back.
steps.hint: `u` is undo. Press it as many times as you need.

title: `d` is a verb
concept: `d` is a verb: delete. On its own it does nothing — it waits for a noun. `dw` deletes a word, `d$` deletes to the end of the line, and doubling the verb (`dd`) applies it to the whole line. Verb plus noun: that is Vim's whole grammar, starting here.

# Draft

This draft sentence is filler and must go.
Keep this line.

steps.instruction: The cursor is on `draft`. Delete that word with `dw`.
steps.hint: `d` then `w`: delete, then the word noun. Type them one after the other.

steps.instruction: Now delete everything from here to the end of the line with `d$`.
steps.hint: Same verb, different noun: `d` then the `$` you learned as "end of line".

steps.instruction: Delete this whole line with `dd`.
steps.hint: Doubling a verb applies it to the line: `dd`.

title: `c` is delete-then-type
concept: `c` is change: it deletes exactly what `d` would have, then drops you straight into Insert mode so you can type the replacement. Same grammar, same nouns — `cw` changes a word, `cc` changes the whole line.

steps.instruction: The cursor is on `this`. Replace that word with `cw`.
steps.hint: `c` then `w`. Notice the mode badge flips to INSERT — start typing.

steps.instruction: Now replace the entire line with `cc`.
steps.hint: Double the verb for the whole line — `cc`, exactly like `dd`.

title: Copy and paste, Vim's way
concept: `y` yanks — Vim's word for copy — and `yy` yanks a whole line. `p` puts it back after the cursor, `P` before it. Copy and paste in two keystrokes, no modifier keys.

steps.instruction: Copy this whole line with `yy`. Nothing visible happens — that is correct.
steps.hint: `yy` is the yank twin of `dd`: doubled verb, whole line.

steps.instruction: The line is copied. Paste it below with `p`.

title: Numbers multiply commands
concept: Every command takes a count. `3w` jumps three words, `2dd` deletes two lines. Say the number first, then the command — the number multiplies whatever follows, so you never have to learn a separate command for "do it three times".

steps.instruction: Jump three words forward in one go: press `3` then `w`.
steps.hint: Type the digit first, then the motion — `3w`, not `w3`.

steps.instruction: Delete two lines at once: press `2` then `dd`.
steps.hint: The count goes in front of the whole command: `2dd`.

title: Text objects: the noun that finds itself
concept: `iw` means "inner word" — the word you are standing in, no matter WHERE in it you are standing. `aw` is "a word", including the space after it. Pair one with a verb and you get `diw`: delete this word, from anywhere inside it. You stop aiming; you just name the thing.
document:
# Cleanup

The very very quick fox.

steps.instruction: The cursor is in the middle of the first `very`. Delete just that word with `diw`.
steps.hint: Three keys: `d` (delete) `i` (inner) `w` (word). Notice you did not have to move first.

steps.instruction: Now use `daw` — the same thing, but it takes the trailing space too.
steps.hint: Swap the `i` for an `a`: `daw`. Look at the spacing it leaves behind.

title: Quotes are a noun too
concept: The same shape works on quotes: `i"` is everything INSIDE the quote marks, `a"` includes the marks themselves. `di"` empties a quoted string from anywhere on the line — this is the command that makes people fall in love with Vim.

steps.instruction: Empty the quoted title with `di"` — delete inside quotes.
steps.hint: `d` `i` then the `"` key (Shift-apostrophe). The quote marks survive.

steps.instruction: Do it once more — `di"` is worth burning into your fingers.
steps.hint: Same three keys: `d` `i` `"`.

steps.instruction: On the author line, use `da"` to take the quote marks as well.
steps.hint: `a` instead of `i` again — around, not inner.

title: Brackets and paragraphs
concept: Learn the shape once and it works everywhere: `i(` is inside the parentheses, `a(` includes them, `ip` is a paragraph and `ap` a paragraph plus the blank line after it. Same verbs, new nouns — nothing new to memorise.
document:
Ring the bell(twice) at noon.

This paragraph is scratch.
Delete the whole thing.

Keep this one.

steps.instruction: Copy the bracketed bit, brackets included, with `ya(`.
steps.hint: `y` (yank) `a` (around) `(`. The document should not change — it is a copy.

steps.instruction: Now empty the brackets but keep them, with `di(`.
steps.hint: `d` `i` `(` — inner, so the brackets stay behind.

steps.instruction: Delete this whole scratch paragraph — and the blank line after it — with `dap`.
steps.hint: `d` `a` `p`. A paragraph is any run of lines between blank lines.

steps.instruction: Try `dip` instead — inner paragraph, leaving the blank line in place.
steps.hint: `d` `i` `p`. Compare the blank lines with what `dap` left.

title: The grammar clicks
concept: Here is the whole language: VERB + MODIFIER + NOUN. `d` + `i` + `w` is delete inner word. Swap any single piece — `c` for `d`, `"` for `w` — and you have a command you never had to learn. That is why Vim users say they are not memorising; they are speaking.

# Release note

Vimkin ships with a "TODO tagline" and a zzz stray word.

steps.instruction: Start from the verb you know: delete the placeholder word with `diw`.
steps.hint: `d` `i` `w` — the cursor is already inside the word.

steps.instruction: Now swap ONLY the verb: `ciw` deletes it and lets you type the replacement.
steps.hint: One letter changed: `c` instead of `d`. Everything else is identical.

steps.instruction: Now swap ONLY the noun: `ci"` rewrites the quoted tagline.
steps.hint: `c` `i` `"`. Same verb as `ciw`, a different noun — and it just works.
